 Congress 
 Another looming funding deadline for federal agencies, what happens when the current CR expires
 "Many, especially progressive Democrats, have indicated they don't want any part of approving any kind of money for the war," said Mitchell Miller.
 Terry Gerton 
 November 16, 2026 3:21 pm 
 8 min read 
 Guest: 
 Mitchell Miller 
 Title: 
 Capitol Hill correspondent, WTOP 
 Summary: 
 Another looming funding deadline for federal agencies…with just a few weeks left for Congress to decide what’s next after the current continuing resolution expires. And there’s a new complication – discussions to potentially add Defense Department funding via a budget reconciliation package. Meanwhile, Congressional Democrats are putting together their oversight plans for the next Congress that starts in January. 
 The Federal Drive with Terry Gerton provides expert insights on current events in the federal community. Read more interviews to keep up with daily news and analysis that affect the federal workforce. Reach out to Terry and the Federal Drive producers with feedback and story ideas at FederalDrive@federalnewsnetwork.com .
 Interview transcript 
 Jared Serbu All right, Mitchell, and let’s start with the reconciliation news, which I know has been under discussions over the last few days on Capitol Hill. What exactly is the Republican majority along with President Trump aiming to do here?
 Mitchell Miller Well, they’re basically trying to resurrect the budget reconciliation that kind of went to the side, especially after the midterm elections. A lot of people wondered what was going to happen with it. Well, President Trump has made it very clear he wants to bring it back. And he made a big push late last week and said, look, Republicans, I need you on board with this. We need to get this budget reconciliation process moving again. He wants $350 billion for the Defense Department. This would be part of the whole $1.5 trillion budget proposal that is before Congress right now, but he’s really making this last-minute push related to this. What’s interesting is that he got some push back from Republican senators who are worried that if they push too hard for this, that this is going to potentially break up the discussions in connection with regular order and trying to get an agreement before December 11th when the federal spending runs out and we could potentially see a government shutdown and several Republicans last week indicated that if this reconciliation package becomes too much of a dog with a bone type of situation that it could potentially lead to a government shutdown because Democrats have a lot of problems with it. Obviously they’re feeling very emboldened after the elections and they don’t want to Republicans try to push this through on their own. So it’ll be interesting to see how much more the president keeps pushing on this and whether Republicans go along with him. Obviously, he’s lost a little political luster after those elections. So we’ll have to see if this actually makes it forward.
          Join us Dec. 7 at 1 pm for Federal News Network's Industry Exchange IT Modernization event. Top technology leaders will explore the latest IT modernization strategies and share actionable insights to help agencies optimize infrastructure, strengthen security and improve mission outcomes.
 Jared Serbu And not to get too deep into budget procedure here, but I think sort of the regular order way to do this would be a supplemental appropriation or an overseas contingency operations budget to fund effectively an ongoing war. But I guess the advantage of doing it through reconciliation is you only need 50 votes in the Senate, is that the rationale here?
 Mitchell Miller Exactly. And also complicating that factor is the war. Democrats have indicated, many, especially progressive Democrats, have indicated they don’t want any part of approving any kind of money for the war, they want to stop it in its tracks. Now, some more moderate Democrats have indicated a bit more willingness to work with Republicans in terms of funding the conflict with Iran. But a lot of Democrats have said that’s just a non-starter for them. So that’s on the other side of the aisle. That’s potentially another problem as well in connection with looking at a shutdown. If they get in too much of a standoff in connection arguments over whether money is going to go to the war effort, we could see a stand off there. So they would like to get some kind of longer term agreement as they always want to, but whether they actually do, we’ll have to see. It could still very well end up being some type of continuing resolution. That moves into the next year. Of course, a lot of Republicans, particularly conservatives, don’t want that to happen because they want to use the last bit of power that they have here in the lame duck session.
 Jared Serbu And is this the major factor at this point that’s leading to speculation about a potential shutdown? Would we be seriously looking at that prospect if it weren’t for this dispute over defense funding?
 Mitchell Miller Yeah, I think it’s definitely the central factor, no question about it. Really, a lot of the lawmakers, as is often the case, don’t want to shut down. They don’t want to have another showdown. They, we had so many shut down showdowns over the last year plus that really people just want to move on from that. They know that voters have clearly made the argument that they don’t this to keep happening over and over again. They want something to actually happen and move forward. On some of these priorities that a lot of voters told lawmakers that they have, both Democrats and Republicans. So I think that’s going to be the central issue, this matter of whether or not this budget reconciliation package comes through and what the position is of Democrats as they move forward with their leadership, which also has its own dynamic because you have now a challenge with Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen (D), challenging Chuck Schumer (NY-D) for the Senate majority leader position. That could also alter things a little bit. Clearly, Schumer has favored to retain his position, but it just shows that there’s a lot of moving parts within the Democratic Party right now.
 Jared Serbu And then also looking forward to the next Congress, the Democrats are going to have a large list of oversight priorities. How is that starting to take shape at this early stage?
 Mitchell Miller Well, you have the House Oversight Committee that will be led by Richard Garcia, who has made it very clear that he wants to hold the administration to account on a lot of issues, whether it’s the Epstein files or looking into matters of alleged corruption within the government and the administration. There’s talk about reviewing what DOGE did and whether or not it really got the savings that were claimed by Elon Musk and others. And then you also have the House Judiciary Committee, which is likely to be led by Maryland Democrat, Jamie Raskin, I spoke to him last week and he was among the Democrats that are really upset about this new challenge from the administration that came out through the White House Council and through the president himself saying, wait a second, if you’re talking about all this oversight in these investigations, you better hold off because we potentially could hold you criminally liable if you do something that goes too far investigating the administration. Now, Democrats literally laughed this off in some respects because they said, look, Jamie Raskin pointing out that the previous administration under President Biden, as well as his son, Hunter Biden, were obviously the focus of huge oversight investigations related to allegations of the Biden crime family, etc. Issue though for Democrats is to balance that as we’ve been hearing a lot over the last few weeks with affordability and accountability. They don’t want to make their whole agenda look like it’s only about going after the administration or going after The White House. They want to investigate corruption obviously, but they also feel like they have to do some things legislatively in terms of trying to bring down costs. So that will be one of their challenges moving forward.
 Jared Serbu And that aggressive posture that the administration has taken toward, you know, prospective congressional investigations, have Democrats started to talk about how they’re going to grapple with the fact that they are definitely not going to get any kind of cooperation from the justice department in terms of doing things like enforcing subpoenas?
          Sign up for our daily newsletter so you never miss a beat on all things federal
 Mitchell Miller Yeah, I think they’re very much ready for that. People like Jamie Raskin, who’s a former constitutional scholar, knows that this is likely coming. He has experience with this in connection with the January 6th investigation, for example. Democrats tried over and over again to get various people within the administration to testify, and there were all these legal battles. And I think that’s what you’re going to see. A lot more of, especially with Stephen Miller now installed as the White House Chief of Staff. They are not going to give an inch at the White House on these requests. Now, of course, with oversight, the Democrats in power in the Senate and in the House, when they come in in January, they will have legitimate power to do all of this. But I think you’re going to see, once again, what we saw a few years ago, where you’re going to have these legal battles going back and forth. And then Democrats will have to decide, as they did during that earlier period. Do they just continue to fight with trying to get subpoenas and getting people before various committees, or do they back off a little bit and try to do other things? I think the line that a lot of lawmakers are using is we can walk and chew gum at the same time, but it is going to be a balance for them because it can, as you know, take up a lot of time when you’re trying to get somebody, for example, in front of a committee, and they cite executive privilege, for examples, so. Those are the kind of fights I think we’re going to be seeing definitely in the coming months.
